stops.name: Famagusta, born to the triad of the Levant
stops.campa: Catherine is born about the year 290 in Famagusta, daughter of Costus, the Cypriot king of that harbor city. In this same decade and this same stretch of the Levant, two other daughters are born who will be remembered beside her forever after: Margaret at Antioch on the Orontes, Barbara at Heliopolis under the shadow of Baal's great temple, some two hundred kilometers apart. The three will never meet in the flesh, yet the tradition binds them as sisters: the virgin martyrs, a variation of the three magic sisters of the old fairy-tale pattern, born within one decade of one another, each unknowing of the other two.

stops.name: Famagusta: the child begins her study of the stars and the tongue
stops.campa: At eight years old, while other daughters of the Cypriot court are set to needlework, Catherine is set to tutors. She takes up rhetoric and the sciences of the Greeks: the trivium of grammar, logic, and persuasion, the study of the stars and of number. She outpaces every master her father brings to the palace. The library of Famagusta empties into her memory. Even as a child she argues points of philosophy with visiting scholars and unsettles them with the precision of her questions, so that Costus begins, half in pride and half in unease, to call her his small oracle.

stops.name: Famagusta, the death of Costus, the crown at fourteen
stops.campa: Costus dies when Catherine is fourteen, and the court of Famagusta, having no son to set on the throne, crowns his daughter queen in his place. She rules with the same exactness she brought to her books, hearing petitions, weighing law, and refusing the counselors who would marry her off within the month to steady the kingdom with a husband's hand. She tells her court that no man she has yet met matches her in learning, and that she will not be given to a mind smaller than her own: queen and scholar in one small body, already unwilling to be ruled.

stops.name: Famagusta: the court presses her toward Alexandria
stops.campa: Her counselors will not let the question of marriage rest, and Catherine at last gives them an answer that satisfies no one but herself: she will go to Alexandria, where the great libraries still stand, scarred by fire but largely whole in this fourth century, and where, among philosophers and princes both, she may yet find a mind and a rank to match her own, or find neither and remain as she is. The court reads this as consent and begins to prepare ships and a household. Catherine reads it as a door opening onto something she cannot yet name.

stops.name: The sea road south, Cyprus to Egypt
stops.campa: The queen of Famagusta takes ship south across open water, her household and her books stowed below with her, the Cypriot coast falling away behind and the low shore of Egypt not yet risen ahead. She keeps to the deck through the crossing, unrestful, watching the horizon the way she once watched a page of Euclid: for the line where one thing resolves into another. She does not yet know that she sails toward a hermit, a wilderness, and a marriage no earthly court could have arranged for her; she knows only that Famagusta was too small a proof for what she is.

stops.name: Alexandria, the palace and the libraries, scarred but standing
stops.campa: Catherine comes ashore at Alexandria, greatest port of learning in the world, and takes a palace among its philosophers and princes. The great collections have suffered fire in living memory, yet in this fourth century the libraries stand largely intact, their halls still crowded with the scrolls of Euclid and Ptolemy and a hundred lesser hands. She walks the Mouseion's colonnades as a scholar rather than a tourist, calling for texts by name, correcting a copyist's error in passing, and within a season the librarians speak of the young Cypriot queen the way they speak of their own masters: with respect, and a little fear.

stops.name: Alexandria, the suitors turned away
stops.campa: Word of the learned queen spreads through Alexandria's courts, and suitors come: sons of prefects, a philosopher or two, once a nephew of the emperor's own household. Catherine receives each with the same courteous rigor she gave the doctors of Famagusta: she sets them a problem, a point of logic or astronomy, and watches them fail it. None matches her, and she says so plainly, without cruelty but without softening either. Her mother's old confidante, a woman of the palace who has kept a private Christian faith through every reign, watches this parade of failures and begins, quietly, to pray for the girl.

stops.name: Alexandria, the hermit at the palace gate
stops.campa: A hermit comes down out of the desert margin and is admitted to Catherine's palace, sent, he says, by no one but God. He is threadbare, sun-blackened, and entirely unimpressed by her crown. He tells her of a bridegroom fairer than any philosopher's son, wiser than her tutors, born of a virgin and crucified under a governor not unlike her own suitors' fathers. Catherine, who has dismissed a dozen princes on points of logic, finds she cannot dismiss this one point: that she has never yet met her match, and here is a stranger promising her one at last, in the wilderness.

stops.name: The desert beyond Mareotis, the mysteries revealed
stops.campa: The hermit takes Catherine out past Lake Mareotis into the desert margin where the city's noise cannot follow. Here, under a sky she has studied all her life but never truly watched, he opens to her the Christian mysteries one by one: the single God in three persons, the Word made flesh, the cross as victory rather than shame. She interrogates each point the way she once interrogated her tutors, and each time the old man's answer holds. By the second day she has stopped arguing and started listening, which for Catherine of Famagusta is the nearest thing to a conversion the world has yet seen from her.

stops.name: The desert oratory: the Child turns away
stops.campa: In the hermit's small oratory Catherine is shown, in a vision granted through his prayer, the Virgin holding her infant son and is told that this is the bridegroom promised her. She kneels, expecting recognition. Instead the Child turns his face from her and will not look upon her, for she does not yet carry the seal of baptism, and no bride comes unwashed to such a marriage. Catherine, who has never in her life been refused, rises from that oratory floor shaken in a way no failed suitor and no philosopher's argument ever managed, and asks the hermit, urgently now, to be made ready.

stops.name: The desert font, the baptism
stops.campa: The hermit instructs her through the days remaining and, at a spring in the desert margin, baptizes the queen of Famagusta with his own hands, water carried up in an earthen jar because no font stands out here but the ground itself. Catherine goes under confessing the Trinity and rises a Christian, the crown of Cyprus now the smaller of the two crowns she carries. She asks nothing further of the world she left behind: not her palace, not her libraries, not the suitors she turned away, only to be brought back to the oratory, to see whether the Child will look at her now.

stops.name: The desert oratory, the mystical marriage, the ring
stops.campa: Brought again before the vision, Catherine finds the Child's face turned toward her at last, the Virgin smiling beside him amid a great crowd of angels and all the celestial court. The infant Christ takes her hand as a bridegroom takes a bride's, and in token of the marriage sets a ring upon her finger, bidding her keep it in remembrance always. Catherine wakes in the hermit's oratory with the ring still cold and real on her hand, a mark no suitor's gift ever left on her, and understands that she is now betrothed beyond the reach of any earthly emperor's offer.
stops.quote: And there our Lord espoused her in joining himself to her by spiritual marriage, promising ever to keep her in all her life in this world, and after this life to reign perpetually in his bliss, and in token of this set a ring on her finger.
stops.quote_source: Golden Legend (Jacobus de Voragine, trans. William Caxton, 1483), Life of Saint Catherine
